a vessel and the parts assigned

Active Stage Resources:\nShows the resources this active stage \nis consuming.
Empty Stage:\nReady to have parts dragged into it.
Most parts have a contextual menu that lets \nyou interact with them. You will see details \nof the part and any actions you can perform.
Using the time controls you can adjust, or "warp" time as well as toggle \nbetween mission elapsed time (MET) and universe time (UT).
Kerbals on EVA also have contextual actions \nthey can perform. There are some examples \nin the picture here.
Below is the main flight interface. You will be spending a lot of time here, so there is more information \nabout each labeled area in the following pages.
It is inevitable that you will have to manage heat in your space program. Hopefully this info can help.

Both types of radiators require EC to run 
the pumps, but thermal control systems 
are deployable parts, so you also need 
some EC to extend them.
They, like the radiator panels, pump heat from both \nparts and core modules, but do not have the same \n"nearby" parts limitation.
In this example the TCS radiator draws heat from all the parts in the vessel through "pipes" to radiate it to the environment.
Note: Largest size TCS is simply too big to show here.
These parts pump liquid throughout the entire vessel \nto draw heat to the panels.
There is another type of heat generating part. Some parts have \na core component which has another important function (for \nexample drills and ISRU converters).

To keep the core from overheating you will 
need radiators as the part soak is simply not 
enough to prevent an issue.

Luckily, that's whats next.
Note: The flow of heat is not instantaneous. The transfer of energy happens over time.
* Body radiation not shown to save space.
Getting to the Core of It

Engines consume resources and convert that to thrust, with a lot of 
heat generated in the process. Most of that heat leaves the vessel as 
exhaust, so we don't have to worry about that, but some of it does 
"soak" into the engine part itself.

It can be helpful to think of the heat 
production being a module inside the 
internals (like the combustion chamber). 

The exhaust takes a lot of heat away, but 
some of it soaks into the part as well.
